text: Got the call from the vet at four and Pickle's bloods are clear. Completely clear. I'd spent the whole day doing that thing where you don't let yourself hope, I'd even looked up the cost of the treatment and started a mental list of who could cover my shifts, and then the receptionist said 'all normal, nothing to worry about' in the most ordinary voice and I had to sit down on the stairs. He's thirteen. He's been off his food for a fortnight and I'd convinced myself. I drove to the surgery to pick him up and he came out wagging that ridiculous tail as if he'd been at a party, and the nurse said he'd eaten two whole pouches, and I laughed so loudly the waiting room looked up. We're going to the beach on Sunday. He's going to roll in something dead and I'm going to let him.

Sunita came round with the baby this afternoon and I got to hold him for an hour while she slept on my sofa, properly slept, mouth open, for the first time since he arrived by the look of her. He's got her frown. He did this long slow blink at me like he was deciding whether I was worth the bother, and then he grabbed my finger and didn't let go, and I just sat there in the window with the light going gold on his head and felt something in me go quiet and bright at the same time. I didn't check my phone once. When she woke up she apologised about forty times and I told her to come every day if she wanted. She might. I hope she does. There are still two tiny socks under my coffee table and I've left them there on purpose.

The reunion I'd been dreading for three months turned out to be one of the best nights of the year. Fifteen years since school and I'd built it up into some kind of exam where I'd be marked on my job and my waistline, and within ten minutes of walking in Callum had me crying with laughter about the time we got locked in the science cupboard. Nobody asked what anyone earned. Nobody cared. We were just those same people with slightly worse knees, telling the same stories and finding they'd got better with age. Meera and I talked for an hour in the car park afterwards about everything and nothing, the way we used to on the bus, and swapped numbers like we meant it this time. Got home at one. Can't stop grinning. Why did I think I'd outgrown these people?

The strawberries came good. I know how that sounds, but I planted those runners in March in a bed the slugs had claimed as their own, I netted them, I watered them in the heatwave with the washing-up water because of the hosepipe ban, and this morning Ines and I went out in our pyjamas and picked a whole colander full, warm from the sun, and ate half of them standing in the garden with juice on our chins. She's seven and she looked at me like I'd done a magic trick. We made a very bad jam in the afternoon that didn't set and it is still the best jam I've ever tasted. The kitchen smells of it. Her hands are pink. I feel ten feet tall and about nine years old at the same time.

The flight was delayed two hours, the taxi driver got lost, and I did not care about any of it because at the end of all that was Ngozi's kitchen with the radio on and a pot of jollof going and three people shouting over each other about whose turn it was to lay the table. I haven't been home for Christmas in four years. Four years of work excuses and expensive flights and 'next year, definitely'. Mum pretended not to be crying and then stopped pretending. My little cousins have become actual people with opinions. Uncle Femi still tells the same story about the goat and it is still funny. I slept in my old room with the window that doesn't quite shut and woke up to the sound of the compound gate and a cockerel and I lay there with my eyes closed, just listening, happier than I've been in a long time.

We've been trying to get the band back in a room for two years and tonight it finally happened. Dario's garage, same as when we were nineteen, same broken amp that only works if you lean a chair against it. We were terrible for the first half hour, honestly dreadful, nobody could remember the bridge of anything. And then Liv counted in the old one, the first song we ever wrote, and something clicked and we played it straight through and at the end we all just looked at each other. Forty-three years old, mortgages, two divorces between us, one hip replacement scheduled, and for three and a half minutes we were exactly who we used to be. We've booked the garage for next Thursday. I've been humming it since I got home. My ears are ringing. Worth it.

Bea took her first steps today and I was there for it. I almost wasn't, I'd been about to leave for the gym, and Sol said 'wait, look' in that voice and I turned round and she was standing in the middle of the rug with her arms out like a tiny surfer, wobbling, and then she took one step, and then two, and then sat down hard on her bottom and looked absolutely furious about it. We both cheered so loudly she burst into tears. I've watched the video eleven times. She did it again after lunch, four steps this time, straight to the dog, who put up with it magnificently. I know every parent says this and I know it's just walking and billions of people have done it. I don't care. My girl walked today and I saw it and I will never not have seen it.

The snow came overnight and the whole street was out by eight. Nobody had planned it. Mr Hussain from number twelve had a sledge from about 1985, the twins from the end had a tea tray, and somehow we all ended up on the slope behind the church taking turns like children, adults included, Priti in her work coat screaming the whole way down. I haven't laughed like that since before the pandemic. My trousers were soaked to the thigh. Someone brought out a flask. Someone else started a snowman that got out of hand and is now taller than the postbox. The office is shut, the trains are off, and for one day the world has given everybody permission to just play. My cheeks ache. I'm drying my socks on the radiator and I don't want tomorrow to come and spoil it.

They're closing the library. Forty years it's been there, the one on the corner with the stained glass and the radiator that clanks, and the letter says 'consolidation of services' and gives a date in June. I learned to read in that building. Mrs Achebe, who ran it when I was small, used to let me sit behind the desk and stamp the returns. I took Freya there every Saturday for six years, we had a bench by the window, she chose her books by the colour of the spine. I walked past tonight and it was dark except for the exit sign, and I stood there longer than I meant to. I know it's a building. I know the books will go somewhere else. But it was the one place in this town that asked nothing of me and gave me everything, and I didn't say thank you to it properly, and now I'm not sure how.

Dropped Caleb at the airport at five this morning. Two years in Melbourne, maybe longer, a job he's wanted since he was fifteen, and I'm so proud of him I could burst, and I have been crying on and off since the departures board. I did fine at the gate. I made the jokes. I told him to call his grandmother. Then I walked back through the car park and sat in the car and couldn't find the key for ten minutes because I couldn't see. The house when I got back was exactly the same as when we'd left it except that his cereal bowl was in the sink and I stood there and couldn't wash it. I know he's not gone, not really. We'll talk on Sunday. He's happy. It's the right thing. I just didn't know the air could go out of a house like this.

Found out from Facebook that Nathan died. Nathan from the first job, who taught me how to use the fax machine and shared his sandwiches when I'd forgotten lunch, who had a laugh you could hear across the whole floor. We lost touch when I moved, the way you do, and I'd always assumed we'd bump into each other at something eventually. There's a photo on his page from a wedding last summer. He looks exactly the same. Fifty-one. His daughter posted it, and reading her words I realised I didn't know he had a daughter. Twenty years of thinking 'I must look him up' and now there's nothing to look up. I went for a walk this evening and I kept hearing that laugh. I'm not sure I've got the right to feel this sad about someone I hadn't spoken to in a decade. I do anyway.

Mum didn't know who I was today. She was polite about it, she's always polite, she asked if I was the new girl and whether I'd had far to come. I said not far. I made her tea the way she likes it and she said 'you've done that just how my daughter does it', and I had to go and stand in the corridor. The nurse says it comes and goes and that last week she talked about me for an hour. I know that. I know the person is still in there. But I drove home down the road she taught me to drive on and she wasn't there in the passenger seat telling me to check my mirrors, and she won't be again, not really, and I don't know how you grieve someone who's still alive and asking if you've had far to come. Jamal's run me a bath. I'm going to sit in it until the water goes cold.

Took the ring off today. Not in a dramatic way, I was washing up and it caught on the sponge like it always did, and I put it on the windowsill like always, and then I just didn't put it back on. It's been eleven months. Everyone else moved on around March, I think: they stopped asking, they started inviting me to things as one. I've been the one lagging behind, keeping the chair at the table, keeping his coffee mug at the front of the cupboard. The ring is in the dish with the hair ties now. My hand looks strange. Lighter and wrong. I keep touching the place where it was. I don't feel better and I don't feel worse, I feel like I've put something down that I'd been carrying so long I'd stopped noticing the weight, and now my arm doesn't know what to do.

Chen didn't get in. The letter came this morning and he opened it at the table and read it twice and then folded it very carefully and said 'okay' and went upstairs, and I have never heard a quieter word. He's worked for that place for two years. He's done the extra classes, the weekend sessions, he turned down the trip to Portugal to revise. I wanted to go up and I didn't because he asked me not to, and I've been sitting at the bottom of the stairs ever since, listening to nothing. I can't fix this one. I can't ring somebody. I can't make it a learning experience yet, it's too soon and he'd be right to hate me for trying. I just have to watch my kid be crushed and wait until he's ready to be held. Dinner's gone cold. I'll make something else later.

Last day in the house tomorrow. I walked round every room tonight with the lights off because I wanted to see it the way it looked when the kids were small and I'd check on them: the landing with the loose board, the bathroom where Marta's height marks are still on the door frame in biro, the kitchen where we had every argument and every birthday. The buyers are young and lovely and they talked about knocking through, and I smiled and said what a good idea. I keep telling people it's just bricks. It's not. It's thirty-one years of a life and it's going in a van at eight o'clock and the new place has a lovely garden and a lift and I will be fine. Tonight I sat on the stairs where I used to wait for Nikos to come home and I let myself cry about it properly, once, so I don't do it in front of the movers.

We were going to go to Scotland in October. It was going to be the trip: the sleeper train, the loch Dad always talked about, the pub with the fire. I'd booked it in January as a surprise for his seventieth. I cancelled it this afternoon, sitting in the hospice car park, and the woman on the phone was kind and asked no questions and refunded all of it, which somehow made it worse. He's comfortable. He's not in pain. He knows us most of the time. But he isn't getting on a train, and I'd known that for weeks and today I finally did the admin of knowing it. I didn't tell Mum. She's got enough. I sat in the car and looked at the confirmation email, 'your booking has been cancelled', and thought about the pub with the fire, and the loch, and all the things we'll now never do, and I wasn't ready. I'm still not.

Interview at ten tomorrow for the job I actually want, not the job I'm pretending I'd be fine without. I've done the prep. I've done the prep so many times that I'm now worried I'll sound rehearsed, so I've been un-prepping, which is not a thing, and I know it's not a thing. I rang Lucia to run through my answers and she said they were good and I heard the pause before 'good' and now I'm wondering what the pause meant. My suit's ironed. The route's checked. I know where to park. None of it is helping. My stomach has that hollow churning it gets before exams and I'm thirty-six and it's like I never left school. I keep thinking: if I don't get this, what does that say. Which is not useful. I'm going to try to sleep. I'm going to lie there until two and then sleep badly.

The letter from the bank says 'we'd like to discuss your account' and gives a number, and I've been staring at it for three hours instead of ringing it because as long as I don't ring it I don't know. The overdraft's been sitting at the limit since March. I've been robbing one card to pay the other and telling Dmitri it's all fine, it's just a tight month, and it's been a tight month for six months. I don't even know what they want. Maybe nothing. Maybe it's a form letter. But I've had that heavy sick feeling under my ribs all day, the one that makes food taste of nothing, and when the phone rang at lunch I actually jumped. I'll call in the morning. I've written it on my hand like a child. I just don't know how I'll start the sentence.

Ravi's forty minutes late and his phone's going to voicemail. I know what this is. I know he'll have stopped for petrol, or the motorway's shut, or the phone's dead in his bag like it always is, and he'll walk in and say 'what?' and I'll feel foolish. I know that. I've still checked the traffic site nine times and I've got the news on in the kitchen with the sound down, watching for anything about the M6, which is insane, I'm aware it's insane. My mum did this. She'd stand at the window every time Dad was late and I swore I'd never be her, and here I am at the window. The dinner's drying out in the oven. My hands are cold. I'm going to write this instead of ringing again, because if I ring again and it goes to voicemail again I don't think I'll be able to breathe properly.

They've announced a restructure. That's all the email said, 'restructure', with a meeting on Monday to 'share more detail', and the whole floor went quiet in that way where everyone's reading the same thing at the same time. Nobody said anything. We all just carried on typing. I've been here nine years. I'm the only one on the team who's part-time, and I've done the maths on how that looks on a spreadsheet, and I've done the other maths on the mortgage. Tobias says they'd never let me go, I know too much, which is sweet and not how any of this works. I ate my lunch at my desk because I couldn't face the kitchen chatter. I've been composing a version of my CV in my head since about two. The weekend is going to be very long. I've started grinding my teeth again, I can feel it.

Milo's got his first sleepover tonight, at the Fernandes house, and I am a wreck. He was fine, he practically pushed me out of the door. Lara Fernandes is lovely and sensible and has three kids of her own and a dog and a fire blanket in the kitchen, I checked. I have no reason to be like this. And yet I've been sitting here since seven with the phone face-up on the table, imagining him awake at midnight in a strange bed too shy to say he wants to come home. He's eight. I was sleeping in tents at eight. Jun's gone to bed and said with great patience that I should too, and I will, in a minute, after I've checked the phone one more time and not texted Lara, because I promised I wouldn't text Lara. My neck is tight. I keep looking at the door as if he might come through it.

Exam in nine hours. I've gone through the past papers four times, I've made the cards, I've done the thing where you teach it to an empty chair. And I know, I know, that I know this. But my brain has gone into that loop where it keeps running the scenario where I open the paper and the first question is the one topic I skimmed, and then my mind goes white, and then it's over, and I'm back at square one in September with Dad doing the voice. I can't eat. I had a biscuit at six and it sat there like a stone. Aisha's asleep next door and I can hear her breathing through the wall and I'd give anything for that kind of calm. I've set three alarms. I've laid out the pens. I'm going to lie down and not sleep now.

The scan is next Tuesday and I've been doing that thing again where I google symptoms at two in the morning and then feel sick for the rest of the night. I know I shouldn't. The doctor was calm, almost bored, and said in nine cases out of ten it's nothing, and I believed him in the room. It's at home that it unravels. Every twinge is evidence. I've been avoiding Grace because she'll ask how I am and I'll either lie or cry, and I don't want to do either until I know. Work's been a blessing, honestly, seven hours a day when I'm too busy to think. But then the drive home, and the quiet house, and the week of waiting that stretches out like a corridor. I've started counting breaths at night. In for four, hold for four. It helps for about a minute at a time.

Had to stand up at the parents' meeting tonight and say the thing about the school bus route, and from about four o'clock I could feel my pulse in my throat. I practised it in the car. I practised it in the loo. When they called my name I stood up and my voice came out about an octave higher than I'd planned and I lost my place halfway through the second point and there was a silence that was probably two seconds and felt like a week. People nodded. Hazel said afterwards it was fine, it was good, people agreed with me. Maybe. I've been replaying it ever since, every stumble, and I can feel the heat in my face just thinking about it. I'd rather run a marathon than do that again. I probably will have to do it again. That thought alone has my shoulders up round my ears.

Took the boat out alone for the first time since Dad sold his. Six in the morning, the lake like glass, mist sitting on the water so the far shore wasn't there at all. I rowed out past the buoy and shipped the oars and just drifted. A heron went over, low, and didn't bother about me. For about an hour there was nothing: no phone, no voice in my head listing things, just the drip off the blades and my own breathing and the hull ticking as the sun came onto it. I used to think I needed a reason to be out there. Fishing, or exercise, or clearing my head. I didn't clear anything. I just sat in the middle of a lake and let the day start without me, and when I rowed back my shoulders had come down from wherever they live now. I'll go again on Saturday.

Power cut tonight, the whole street, from about seven. No telly, no router, phones on twenty percent and saved for emergencies. We lit the candles from the drawer, the emergency ones and then the nice ones Nadine got for Christmas that we'd been saving for nothing in particular. Ate bread and cheese at the kitchen table. The kids got bored of complaining after half an hour and then found the cards, and we played rummy by candlelight until nine and the little one fell asleep on the bench with a run of hearts in her hand. The house sounded different, quieter underneath. I could hear the fridge not humming. When the lights came back on at ten we all groaned, honestly groaned, and Nadine went round switching half of them off again. I want to remember how my chest felt tonight. Like something had unclenched that I didn't know was clenched.

Went back to the pool after eighteen months. I'd been putting it off because I knew I'd be slow and I was slow, laughably slow, the woman in the lane next to me was seventy if she was a day and she lapped me twice. I didn't mind. There's something about being underwater that switches the noise off. Just the count of the strokes and the black line and the muffled thump of my own heart. Forty lengths at a pace a child could manage. Afterwards in the changing room I sat on the bench with my hair dripping and realised I hadn't thought about the Henderson contract for forty minutes, which is the longest I've gone in a fortnight. Walked home with wet hair in the cold and didn't care. I'm going on Thursday. I'm going to be slow again and that's going to be fine.

Sunday morning and nobody has anywhere to be. Elias is reading the paper in the chair with his feet on the dog. Rain on the skylight. I made the bread last night so it was just a matter of putting the oven on, and the whole flat smells of it now. We haven't spoken much. We don't need to. He read me a bit from the obituary of some racing driver and I said 'hm' and that was a conversation. I've been so braced lately, with the move and the hospital stuff with his mum and the thing at work, that I'd forgotten my body could do this: just sit, heavy and warm, with a mug going cold on my knee. Nothing's resolved. Monday will come with all of it. But right now there's bread, and rain, and a man reading me obituaries, and that's the whole world.

Finished the last of the chemo paperwork today and filed it in the box, and then sat on the bedroom floor for a long time with my back against the bed. Not crying. Not anything, really. Just still. It's been fourteen months of appointments and forms and holding my breath, and now there's a letter that says 'routine follow-up in six months' and nothing else to fill in. Cass asked what I wanted to do to mark it and I didn't know. I don't want a party. I don't want to go anywhere. I think I just want some ordinary days, lots of them in a row, where the biggest decision is what's for tea. I watered the plants. I put a wash on. I stood at the back door and watched a blackbird for about ten minutes. That felt like enough. That felt like exactly enough.

Long walk on the coast path with no one, which I haven't done in years because there's always been someone who needed me somewhere. Eight miles. The wind was behind me most of the way and the sea was doing that slow grey heave it does in November. I stopped at the bench above the cove and ate my sandwich and watched a woman throw a ball for a dog that had no intention of bringing it back, and I realised I wasn't planning anything. Not dinner, not the week, not what I'd say to Marguerite about the money. My head was just full of sea. I got back to the car with the light going and my face stinging and I sat there a while before I started the engine, not because I was tired, just because I wasn't in a hurry to let the noise back in. I think I need to do this more. I think I've needed it for about a decade.

Sat up with Grandpa on the porch after everyone else had gone in. He doesn't talk much any more and I've stopped trying to make him. We watched the bats come out over the field and he pointed at the first one and then at the second and then just left his hand on the arm of the chair. Crickets. Somebody's sprinkler two gardens over. Rosa's radio very faintly through the kitchen window. I was going to go to bed at ten and then I was going to go at half past and then I stopped looking. He put his hand over mine at one point, briefly, the way he does, and went back to watching the sky. I don't know how many more of these there are. Maybe lots. Maybe not. Tonight I wasn't counting. I was just there, and he was there, and the bats did what bats do.

Day off, and I spent it doing almost nothing on purpose. Woke without an alarm, which I've forgotten the feeling of. Lay there listening to the pigeons on the roof. Made proper coffee with the pot instead of the machine. Read a chapter of the book about the lighthouse keeper on the back step with the sun on my shins. Then at some point I noticed I'd been staring at the fence for twenty minutes watching a spider rebuild something and I didn't feel the slightest urge to be productive about it. Sunny texted to see if I wanted to come to the thing and I said not today and she said 'good for you' with a heart. I made soup. I ate it. I watched the light go round the kitchen. My jaw, which has been clenched since roughly 2019, is not clenched. I'm writing this to remind myself that this exists and I can have it.

I want to write about Ms Okonkwo because I never thanked her and she's retiring on Friday. Year nine. I was the kid at the back who never spoke, whose mum had just left, who'd stopped handing in homework because what was the point. She didn't make a thing of it. She just started writing one line on the bottom of everything I did manage, something specific, 'this sentence is really good' or 'I'd like to know what happens next', and after a term of that I started handing things in to see what she'd write. That's it. That's the whole intervention. And I'm a writer now, actually paid for it, and I think the line goes straight back to a woman with green ink who decided a sullen fourteen-year-old was worth a sentence a week. I sent her a card today care of the school. I hope it reaches her. I hope she knows.

The money arrived this morning. I'd asked Ibrahim for a loan, properly asked, with a repayment plan written out because I was so ashamed, and he'd said 'let me look at it' in a way I took to mean no. And then the transfer came through with the reference 'not a loan' and a text that just said 'sort it out and don't mention it again'. I sat on the kitchen floor. I haven't told anyone how close it was. The eviction letter was for the fourteenth. The kids didn't know. I've spent three weeks smiling at them over cereal with my stomach in knots and lying awake doing sums that didn't add up. I paid it all this afternoon, standing in the bank with my hands shaking, and walked out into the car park and the air was just air again. I'll pay him back whether he wants it or not. I will never, ever forget this.

Tilly's teacher stayed behind for forty-five minutes after school today, on her own time, to talk me through what she's seeing and what we can do about it. She'd made notes. She'd found a specialist who does sliding-scale fees. She said, 'I've been thinking about Tilly on the drive home and I didn't want you to have to figure this out alone.' I don't know this woman beyond parents' evening. She has thirty children in that class and a baby at home, I've seen the photo on the desk. I drove home with Tilly singing in the back and I had to pull over for a second because I was suddenly so full of something I couldn't drive through it. People say the system's broken and it is, but inside it there are people like that, quietly holding other people's kids up with both hands. I'm going to write to the head. I'm going to make sure somebody knows.

I slept through the night. All of it. Eleven until half six, no waking, no three a.m. ceiling, and when I opened my eyes the light was already grey at the curtains and for a moment I didn't know where I was. First time in four months, since the accident, since the pills, since the whole business with the insurance. I lay there and felt almost giddy about it. It's such a small thing to be grateful for. A night. Tomas had crept out and left a note by the kettle, 'didn't want to wake you', and I made toast and ate it slowly looking at the garden and I felt like a person who could do a Tuesday. Thank you, body. Thank you, whatever shifted. I know it might not happen again tonight. I'm taking this one and holding it up to the light.

My daughter turned eighteen today and I keep thinking about the nurse in the special care unit who, nineteen years ago on a night I was sure I'd lose both of them, pulled up a chair next to my wife's bed and said, 'I'm not going anywhere, you two sleep.' I never got her surname. She was on nights that week and then she wasn't and by the time I thought to ask, the ward had changed. Tonight Ama blew out her candles in a kitchen full of people who love her, loud and tall and absolutely certain of herself, and Fola squeezed my hand under the table and I knew she was thinking about the same chair. We don't talk about it. We don't need to. Somewhere there's a woman in her sixties now who gave us a night's sleep and a daughter and has no idea. I hope her life has been kind to her. I hope someone sat with her, once, when she needed it.

The van broke down on the dual carriageway at eleven at night with all the stock in the back and the show at nine the next morning, and I rang Oisin on the off chance and he was there in thirty-five minutes with a tow rope and a flask. He'd been in bed. He didn't say so, I only know because his jumper was on inside out. We got the van to his yard, moved everything into his trailer, and he drove me and two hundred jars of chutney to the showground at six in the morning and then went to work. He wouldn't take petrol money. He said 'you'd do it for me' and I would, I absolutely would, but I'm not sure I'd have done it without a sigh. I had the best day of trading I've had all year and every jar that sold I thought: this is Oisin's. I'm going to find a way to make this up to him that he can't refuse.

Every morning for a month Dad has walked round to mine before his own breakfast to let the dog out, because I couldn't get down the stairs on the crutches, and every morning he's pretended it's on his way to the shop, which it isn't, the shop's the other direction. He's seventy-six. He's got his own knees to think about. Today was the first day I could do it myself and he turned up anyway, and stood at the bottom of the stairs while I came down one step at a time, not helping, just there, and when I got to the bottom he said 'right then' and went to put the kettle on. That's my dad. That's thirty-eight years of my dad in one sentence. I don't tell him often enough. I tried this morning and he said 'don't be soft' and gave me a biscuit. I'm writing it here instead.

I want to remember that Yuki came. The others sent flowers and messages and they meant them, I know they did, but Yuki got on a train for three hours with a bag of groceries and a change of clothes and didn't ask if it was okay. She just arrived. She cooked. She didn't make me talk about the miscarriage and she didn't tiptoe round it either, she just was there in my kitchen frying onions and swearing at the hob like a normal Thursday. When I did cry she sat next to me on the floor and said nothing useful and it was exactly right. She slept on the sofa and left at six for work and I found she'd filled the freezer with labelled boxes. I don't know how to thank someone for that. I don't think you can. I think you just try to be that person for someone else, one day, when it's their turn.

Third contractor in a row has quoted for the bathroom and then vanished. Not a no. Not a 'sorry, too busy'. Just silence, after I've taken an afternoon off to show them round, after they've measured everything and nodded and said they'd 'get something over by Friday'. It's been six weeks since the ceiling came down and we're still washing in a bowl in the kitchen. I don't understand what the game is. If you don't want the job, say so, I'll ring the next number on the list. Simi rang the first one again today and his wife answered and said he's 'very busy at the moment', as if we'd been pestering. I've been polite to all of them. I've been patient. I'm now looking at a fourth name and I can already feel myself bracing for the same thing. I'd do it myself if I had the first idea how.

The build has failed eleven times today on a test that passes on my machine, on Petra's machine, on everyone's machine except the one that counts. I've changed nothing. I've reverted everything I changed anyway, in case. I've read the logs so many times I could recite them and they say the same unhelpful thing every time. The deploy was meant to go at four. It's now half seven and there are three people waiting on me in the chat with those little typing dots appearing and disappearing. I know it's some environment thing. I know in two days I'll find it and it'll be a trailing slash or a time zone and I'll laugh. I am not laughing now. I've been grinding my teeth since lunch and I've drunk four coffees and I just want one thing, one thing, to work today the way it's supposed to.

Asked Lars for the third time to put the laundry basket back in the bathroom when he's done with it, and for the third time it is sitting in the hall with one sock in it. I know. I know it's a laundry basket and there are children starving. But it's not the basket. It's that I say a thing, clearly, nicely, and it goes in and apparently nowhere, and I'm left choosing between doing it myself and saying nothing, or saying something and being the nag. I don't want to be the nag. I've watched my mother be the nag for forty years and I swore. And yet here I am at eleven at night writing about a basket. He's lovely. He does loads. This is not about the basket. It is a little bit about the basket. I'm going to move it and go to bed and say nothing and that is not the win it sounds like.

The physio exercises aren't working and I am so sick of doing them. Three times a day, eighteen minutes, the same twelve movements with the band, and the knee is exactly where it was in August: fine on the flat, agony on stairs, locks when I sit too long. The physio says be patient, it's a slow one, some knees take a year. A year. I've had to give up the five-a-side, I've had to give up the hills, I've had to ask Beni to carry the shopping like I'm ninety. I did them all today anyway, every rep, muttering, with the dog watching me from the sofa like I'd lost my mind. Nothing. Not better, not worse. I don't even get the satisfaction of it hurting more so I could say it's doing something. Just the same dull grind and the same stairs tomorrow. I'm going to do them again at eight because I'm not giving up. I'm just allowed to hate it.

Two hours in the queue at the passport office, with the appointment I'd booked, with every document the website listed, and the man behind the glass looked at my birth certificate and said it was the 'short form' and they needed the 'long form', which is mentioned nowhere, nowhere, on any page I read, and I read them all, twice, the night before. Come back when you have it. The flight's on the twentieth. Ordering the long form takes fifteen working days. He shrugged. He actually shrugged, and said he didn't make the rules, which is the sentence I hate most in the English language. I walked out into the rain and rang Sabine and I was so angry I couldn't get the words in the right order. There's an expedited thing. It costs more, of course it does. I'll do it. I'll do all of it. I just want to go back in there and ask him where exactly it said long form.

Mum has decided she doesn't want the carers any more. She told them herself, this morning, without telling me, and they rang me at work to say they'd been 'asked not to come back'. So I drove over at lunch and she was perfectly cheerful and said she manages fine, which she does not, she has not managed fine since the fall, there is a reason the carers were there. I tried everything. Reasonable. Gentle. Firm. She did the thing where she nods and agrees and then says 'but I don't need them' as if we hadn't just spent twenty minutes on it. I love her. I understand it's about dignity. And I'm the one who'll get the call at two in the morning when she's on the kitchen floor again, and she knows that, and she still won't budge. Priyanka says pick your battles. This is the battle. I don't know how to win it without becoming someone she resents.

Nine emails from the client today, each one changing the brief slightly, each one starting with 'just a small thought' and ending with a deadline that hasn't moved. The logo that was approved on Monday is now 'not quite us'. The colour they chose is now 'a bit much'. I've done four versions of the homepage and I'm fairly sure version two is the one they'll end up with, but we have to walk all the way round the houses first because someone's cousin had an opinion. I don't mind revisions, that's the job. I mind pretending that each new direction is a small thought when it's two days' work. Omar says to bill them for every round and he's right and I will. It doesn't stop the feeling of wading through treacle in a straight line towards nothing. I've closed the laptop. It's still open in my head.

Fourth time the referral has bounced back. 'Insufficient information', it says, though the GP has filled in the same form the same way four times and nobody can tell us what's missing. Each bounce is another three weeks. Each three weeks Dev gets a bit quieter and a bit thinner and I get a bit more like a person I don't want to be on the phone. I was sharp with the receptionist today. She didn't deserve it, she's as stuck as we are, and I apologised, but I could hear my voice going up and I hated it. There's a version of me that would write a calm letter to the practice manager and I'm going to try to be that person tomorrow. Tonight I'm just furious at a system that treats a sick sixteen-year-old as a paperwork problem. I've started a file. Dates, names, what was said. I'm going to need it.

Eleven days until the first gig. First proper one, not an open mic, not the back of a pub, a venue with a name and a door person and a poster with our name on it, in print, third from the bottom but on it. Kofi's been sending me set lists at two in the morning. I've rehearsed the thing in the shower so often the neighbours probably know the words. I can't eat properly. Not nerves exactly, more like my body has decided food is an interruption. I walked past the venue on the way to work today, I didn't need to, it's a ten-minute detour, and just stood outside looking at the poster like a tourist. Someone's going to pay money to be in a room while we play. Real people. I keep doing that thing where I get a jolt in my chest remembering. Eleven days. I've already picked the shirt.

The keys are in my pocket. Our keys, to our flat, that is ours, with our names on the deeds and a mortgage that will outlive us both. We walked round it tonight with no furniture and the echo of our own voices and Zahra lay flat on the living room floor and said 'this bit of carpet is mine' and I lay down next to her and we stayed there until it got dark, planning where the shelves would go. There's a crack in the bathroom ceiling. The kitchen tap drips. I love all of it. I've been renting since I was nineteen, fourteen landlords, fourteen sets of rules about blu-tack. Tomorrow I'm going to put a nail in a wall just because I can. We're not even moving in until the fifteenth but I don't know how I'm going to sleep in the old place now. I keep taking the keys out and looking at them.

Got the acceptance from the course. The one in Copenhagen, the one I applied to on a Thursday night after two glasses of wine and then spent a month pretending I hadn't. Six months, starting September, a studio of my own and a stipend that'll just about cover rent if I eat a lot of rice. I've never lived anywhere but this town. I've never been on a plane alone. Mum's face when I told her went through about six expressions before it settled on proud, and then she asked if they have good hospitals, which is her way of saying yes. I've been looking at maps all evening. I've learned how to say 'thank you' and 'where is the station'. I can't sit down. I keep standing up to look at the email on the big screen as if it'll say something different, and it doesn't, it says yes. September. Me. Copenhagen.

Finn gets out on Friday. Two years, four months, and the parole board said yes this morning and his solicitor rang me before she rang him because she knew I'd been sitting by the phone since eight. Friday. I've already changed the sheets on the spare bed twice. I've bought the cereal he likes, the terrible sugary one, and the proper coffee, and I've cleared a drawer. I know it won't be easy. I know the first weeks are hard and he'll be strange and quiet and I'll say the wrong thing. I've read the leaflets. But my little brother is going to walk through that door on Friday and sit at my table and I'm going to make him eggs, and I've been crying on and off about it since lunch, the good sort. I'm going to pick him up myself. I've already worked out the route. Three more sleeps.

Booked the adoption centre visit for Saturday. After eighteen months of Lu saying 'maybe when the lease is sorted' and 'maybe when work calms down', she came home tonight and put a printout of a tabby called Admiral on the fridge and said 'him, Saturday, ten o'clock'. I may have screamed a bit. I've already bought a scratching post, which is premature, I know it's premature, the woman at the centre said come and meet him first, but I walked past the pet shop and my legs went in on their own. He's four. He's been there since March. He's got one ear that bends over. I've looked at his picture about forty times. Lu's pretending to be calm about it and I caught her watching a video called 'first week with your rescue cat' with her headphones in. Saturday. Ten o'clock. Admiral.

Fourteen hours until the race. Number's pinned, gels laid out in a row like a surgeon's tray, porridge measured into the pan for five a.m. Two years ago I couldn't run to the end of the road without stopping; tomorrow I'm doing twenty-six point two miles with eight thousand other lunatics and my name on my vest so strangers will shout it. I don't care about the time. I say that, I do slightly care about the time. Ade's coming to mile eighteen with a sign he won't show me. Mum's tracking me on the app and has already asked how to work it three times. I've got that fizzing feeling under my skin that I used to get the night before a holiday. I won't sleep well and it won't matter. Tomorrow I'm going to cross a line I didn't think I was the sort of person who crossed.

Hamid said yes. On the pier, in the wind, with a seagull trying to take the chips, exactly the wrong moment, exactly the right moment. I'd been carrying the ring for three weeks waiting for a sunset and there was no sunset, there was drizzle and a man fishing, and I just did it anyway because I couldn't wait another day. He laughed first. Then he cried. Then he said 'obviously, you idiot' and the man fishing clapped. We rang his mum from the pier and she screamed so loudly the line crackled. We rang mine and she said 'about time'. I've been looking at his hand all evening. It looks right. I can't sit still, I keep walking from room to room picking things up and putting them down. We're getting married. Him and me. Nothing's planned and I don't care. I'm going to be awake till three.

Three days until the twins start nursery and I get, for the first time in two years and four months, six hours a week in which nobody needs me. I've been planning those six hours like a heist. Coffee, hot, sitting down, start to finish. The library, alone, with no one pulling books off the shelves. A swim. A haircut that isn't a trim in the kitchen. I keep catching myself grinning at the calendar. I feel guilty about how excited I am and then I think, no, I've earned this, I've earned this with eight hundred nights of broken sleep. Ines says it'll feel strange at first and I'll miss them and she's probably right. I'll miss them from a café. With a croissant. Reading something that isn't about a hungry caterpillar. Three days. I've already decided what I'm wearing, which is anything without yoghurt on it.

My son asked me tonight why I'm always on my phone, and he asked it the way you'd ask what's for dinner, not accusing, just curious, and I've been thinking about it for three hours. I said work, which is partly true. The rest is that I pick it up whenever there's a gap, any gap, the kettle boiling, the ad break, him getting his shoes on, and I've been doing it so long I'd stopped noticing. My father read the paper at the table and I hated it. I remember thinking he'd rather be anywhere than with us. I don't think that was true of him and it isn't true of me, but Noah can't know that. He just sees the top of my head. I've put the phone in the kitchen drawer tonight. I don't know if it'll last. I know I'd like him to remember my face more than my scalp.

Forty today. I thought I'd feel something sharper about it. Instead I went for a walk before anyone was up and found myself making a sort of inventory. Things I thought I'd have by now and don't: a house with a garden, a book with my name on it, children. Things I have that I never planned: this city, the pottery, Mariam, a group of friends who'd drive through the night for me. The list of what I haven't done is longer than I'd like and I noticed, walking, that it doesn't ache the way it did at thirty-five. I don't know if that's wisdom or just tiredness. Maybe they're the same thing from different angles. Mariam had made pancakes when I got back and put a candle in the top one, and I made a wish, and for the first time in years I didn't wish for a different life. I wished for more of this one. That felt like news.

Went through the old emails tonight looking for a contract and found the thread with Bruno from 2016, right when things fell apart. I'd remembered myself as the reasonable one. I'd told that story so many times it had set hard. Reading it back, I wasn't. I was cold. I was clever in a way that was really just cruel with better grammar. He kept asking to talk and I kept replying with bullet points. I don't think I was wrong about the business. I think I was wrong about how to be a person while being right about the business. He's doing well now, I hear. I've no plans to get in touch, it's been too long and it would be about me, not him. But I've sat here for an hour with that thread open thinking about the gap between who I think I am and who I am when I'm scared, and it's bigger than I'd like it to be.

The retirement do was tonight and I made a speech that got laughs in the right places and I came home and sat in the car for twenty minutes in the drive. Thirty-four years. I started in that building when the fax machine was new. I've buried two colleagues and been to eleven weddings and seen four bosses come and go, and tomorrow I don't have anywhere to be. People keep asking what I'll do with the time as if time were a problem to be solved. I don't know yet. I'm not sad exactly, I'm not relieved either. It's more like the end of a long film when the lights come up and you blink and the room is a room again. Kirsten's left the hall light on for me. I should go in. I'm just sitting here letting it land. I was somebody in there. I'll find out who I am out here.

My sister and I had the conversation about Mum's house today, the one we've been not having for two years, and it went better than I feared and worse than I hoped. We're not going to fall out over it. We're also not going to be close in the way I always assumed we'd end up, the way sisters are in films. I think I've been waiting for a version of us that was never going to arrive, and today I watched it not arrive and felt mostly calm about it. She's got her life. It's a good one. I'm a visitor in it and she's a visitor in mine and that's allowed. We agreed on the house. We hugged in the car park. On the drive home I kept turning over the fact that the saddest things aren't always the dramatic ones. Sometimes it's just two people being polite about an estate agent.

Our anniversary. Fourteen years. We went to the place by the canal where we had the second date, the first one having been a disaster, and ate the same thing, and talked about the same things, and halfway through I caught myself looking at Teodor across the table and thinking: I don't know this man at all, and I know him better than I know anyone, and both things are true. He's changed. I've changed. The people who met on that first terrible date would probably not like us very much now. We're slower and kinder and much more boring. I used to think love was the fireworks bit at the start. I think now it's the agreeing to keep showing up to the same table as the person across from you quietly becomes someone else. He paid. I'd forgotten my card. Some things don't change.

I lied to Asha today about something small, where I'd been at lunch, and it was so easy that it frightened me. Not because the lie mattered, it didn't, I'd gone to look at a flat on my own and wasn't ready to talk about it. What frightened me was how practised it felt. How my face didn't change. I've been thinking all evening about where I learned that, and I think the answer is my childhood kitchen, where the truth about money or Dad's drinking was never said out loud and everyone got very good at talking about the weather. I'm not that kid any more. I don't need to protect anyone from information. And yet there I was, forty-two, lying about a sandwich. I'm going to tell her tomorrow. About the flat, and about the lie, and probably about the kitchen. I'm not sure how it'll land. I'm sure I'd rather be someone who says it.

Cleaned out my desk at the old place today and the last thing in the drawer was the notebook from my first week, 2011. The first page is a list called 'things to find out' and the last item is 'who do I talk to about staying late'. I read that and laughed and then I didn't. Twelve years of staying late. I got the title and the pay and the glass office with the plant that Jess watered when I forgot, and I'm not sorry about any of it exactly. I'm just noticing, now that I've stopped, how much of it ran on a kind of low hum of wanting to be seen to be enough. The new place is smaller. The job is smaller. I chose that on purpose and I keep having to remind myself I chose it. I've kept the notebook. I'm going to start a new list on the back page and the first item is 'who do I talk to about going home'.
